title: In the Beginning: There Was Prompt Engineering: Part 1
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky offers educators an introduction to prompt engineering as OpenAI and others begin courting teachers with ready-made prompts. He frames it as a mindset of exploration plus a skill, and recommends splitting complex prompts into discrete labelled tasks. Borrowing from rhetorical theory, he builds prompts from audience, context, task and style, and demonstrates with an eleventh-grade civil disobedience activity. He then argues for copious detail when generating quizzes, using a one-question-at-a-time multiple-choice example. He suggests the real benefit for teachers is breaking out of their own habits rather than saving time, and proposes teaching prompt design to students as a lesson in rhetorical situation.
points: Prompt engineering is best approached as an experimental mindset and time spent in the maze, not a shortcut learned from trainers.
Rhetorical-situation elements (audience, context, task, style) give teachers a reusable structure for multi-step prompts.
Generic prompts yield generic quizzes and rubrics, so teachers should start from the end goal and supply detailed specifications.
LLM quiz writing may not save time, but it injects variety beyond a teacher's own implicit patterns.
Prompt design can be taught to students as a way to experience the rhetorical situation first-hand.
quotes: Prompt engineering is an open field of study that everyone can participate in given the right mindset, a time set aside for experimentation, and a little bit of patience.
While AI-trainers and even Substacks like this one may promise you the most direct route through the labyrinth, nothing can replace experimental mindset and actual time in the maze.
Conceptually, the prompt describes or, more accurately, concretizes a “rhetorical situation.” Hey, Purdue OWL, what is a “rhetorical situation”?
Left to its own devices, a LLM will provide you the most generic instructional tools. And then you will have to go many, many rounds with it to get to an instrument that suits your purpose.

Needless to say, one may not be saving any time using a LLM to create quiz questions. The real benefit here is that a teacher can use a LLM to break out of their own implicit rhythms and insert a little randomness into their assessment content.
Through designing their own prompts, students get first-hand experience thinking about the rhetorical situation. Who will be the audience for the task/message generated by the LLM?
